conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My whole job is to look after moms’ emotional health after a baby arrives, and today I’d like to check in with you using a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—the EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. All answers stay between you and me, and there are no right or wrong responses; we just want to be sure you have the right support. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve still been able to laugh sometimes—like when my sister sent that silly meme—but it definitely feels harder than it used to. Most of the day I’m just so tired that even things that should be funny feel kind of flat, so I guess I’d say it’s been more difficult than before the baby came.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not as much as I used to. I can still laugh every now and then—like when my husband made that goofy face at 3 a.m. during a diaper change—but most of the time the tiredness kind of dulls everything, so it feels like I have to force it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve noticed I don’t really look forward to much anymore. I used to get excited about little things—grabbing coffee with a friend, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels like I’m just getting through the next feeding or the next diaper change. I wouldn’t say I’ve lost all enjoyment, but it’s definitely dulled.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for almost an hour and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues.” My partner says I’m too hard on myself, but those thoughts still pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly at night, after I put him down in the bassinet. My mind just races—what if he stops breathing, what if that little cough means he’s getting sick, what if I’m too out of it to hear him cry? There’s no real reason, but I still lie there wide-awake listening to every tiny sound.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but a couple of times—especially when I’m alone with the baby—I’ll get this sudden rush of “what if I can’t handle this?” My heart speeds up and I feel shaky for a minute or two, then it passes. It’s happened maybe twice this week, and there wasn’t any real danger, just my mind jumping to worst-case stuff.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the piles of laundry and the feeding schedule and the constant “what-does-he-need-now” just stack up. I’m not drowning, but I do catch myself thinking, “I can’t keep all these plates spinning,” especially when he skips a nap and the whole routine unravels.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s more the other way around—I’m so tired that I should fall right to sleep, but the second my head hits the pillow my mind starts spinning about the baby, the house, tomorrow’s appointments… so I lie there for an hour or more, then wake up every little sound he makes. I wouldn’t call it “unhappy” keeping me awake so much as racing thoughts and worry.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel sad some of the time—like when I’m rocking him at 2 a.m. and everyone else is asleep. It’s not all day, every day, but little waves of “blue” hit me, especially when I’m exhausted.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice—like when he wouldn’t latch and I felt totally stuck—but I haven’t had any full crying spells this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report, 1 wk post-delivery

Areas of clinical significance  
- Dysthymic mood: intermittent sadness, tearfulness, loss of enjoyment (Q2, Q8)  
- Anxiety/rumination: nocturnal worry about infant safety, mild transient panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Subjective overwhelm / difficulty coping with daily tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems linked to racing thoughts rather than mood (Q7)  

Risk profile  
- No current suicidal ideation or self-harm thoughts (Q10)  
- No anhedonia across all activities; some pleasure preserved  
- Mild-moderate symptom intensity; functional impact limited to fatigue and task-related stress  

Screening impression  
Responses endorse several depressive and anxiety symptoms common in the postpartum period; do not meet threshold for high-risk depression but indicate distress warranting further evaluation and monitoring. Recommend routine follow-up, psycho-education on postpartum mood changes, and consideration of formal assessment (EPDS score and clinical interview) if symptoms persist or worsen.
